title: Hospital Ownership and Public Medical Spending
research_question: How does a hospital's form of ownership — private for-profit, private not-for-profit, or government-owned — shape its response to a large increase in the financial returns to treating low-income patients, and do the resulting changes in hospital behavior translate into improved health outcomes for the indigent?
data_description: The analysis uses administrative data from the California Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development (OSHPD), covering all 397 general acute care hospitals operating continuously in California from 1987 through 1995. Patient-level records contain demographics, zip code of residence, race, insurance status (Medicaid, uninsured, private), and diagnoses for every individual admitted to or born in a California hospital. Hospital-level annual data report finances (revenues by source, costs, net income, subsidies, net worth, property/plant/equipment, financial assets), services offered, employees, bed counts, and ownership type. Disproportionate Share Program (DSH) payments are observed at the hospital-year level. Zip-code-level infant mortality, low-birthweight rates, maternal demographics, and Medicaid coverage shares are constructed for 1382 California zip codes in 1989, 1990, and 1995. All dollar amounts are inflation-adjusted to 1990 dollars.
institutional_context: In 1990, following federal legislation that allowed states to draw federal matching funds, California created a Disproportionate Share Program (DSH) to channel large transfers to hospitals serving many indigent patients. Each of the 23 counties owning a safety-net hospital contributed to a state pool that was matched dollar-for-dollar by the federal government and redistributed to qualifying hospitals. Eligibility hinged on a 'low-income number' — the share of a hospital's costs attributable to Medicaid and uninsured patients — exceeding a 25 percent threshold, with per-diem reimbursements rising nonlinearly from $240 to $1,052 above the cutoff. Roughly $1.7 billion flowed annually, raising qualifying hospitals' revenues by about 45 percent. The threshold and nonlinear schedule sharply altered the marginal profitability of admitting Medicaid patients, especially for hospitals near or above the cutoff. California's hospital sector contained roughly equal numbers of for-profit, not-for-profit, and government (county) facilities, with public hospitals historically serving a disproportionate share of Medicaid and uninsured patients.
